```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(spawnR)
```

When candidate mothers and candidate fathers are sampled separately, the usual
questions are which mother, which father, and which pair. In a hatchery or a
controlled breeding programme there is a better question still: the crosses are
written down, so *which of the crosses that were actually made* did this
offspring come from? `assign_trios()` answers all of them. Everything below is
computed when the vignette is built.

## A small hatchery

Ten dams and ten sires, six microsatellites with four alleles each (a
deliberately weak panel, so that the choices matter), 1% genotyping error, and
80 offspring from random pairings. The crosses that produced them are the
mating design.

```{r}
sim <- simulate_population(n = 20, n_loci = 6, n_alleles = 4,
                           n_offspring = 80, error = 0.01, seed = 2024)
g <- sim$genotypes
p <- allele_freqs(g, reference = c(sim$dams, sim$sires), min_freq = 0.01)
crosses <- unique(data.frame(mother = sim$pedigree$dam,
                             father = sim$pedigree$sire))
nrow(crosses)
```

## Without the crosses

Every mother, every father and every one of the 100 mother-by-father pairs is
scored. Significance comes from the Delta criterion of Marshall et al. (1998),
simulated with the same pool sizes.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
a <- assign_trios(g, sim$offspring, mothers = sim$dams, fathers = sim$sires,
                  freqs = p, error = 0.01, nsim = 3000, nsim_trio = 1000)
summary(a)
```

The printed table carries, for each of mother, father and trio, the LOD,
Delta, the confidence level reached and the number of loci at which each parent
is excluded by Mendelian inheritance alone:

```{r}
head(a[, c("offspring", "mother", "mother_mismatches", "father",
           "father_mismatches", "trio_mother", "trio_father", "trio_delta",
           "trio_mismatches", "trio_confidence")])
```

## With the crosses

Supplying `crosses` restricts the trio analysis to the pairs that were made.
The significance simulation reproduces the actual design, the same parents and
the same pattern of who was crossed with whom, so a simulated runner-up is
usually a half-sib cross sharing one parent with the true one, just as in the
data.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
ac <- assign_trios(g, sim$offspring, freqs = p, error = 0.01,
                   crosses = crosses, nsim = 3000, nsim_trio = 1000)
```

Against the true pedigree:

```{r}
truth <- sim$pedigree[match(sim$offspring, sim$pedigree$offspring), ]
right <- function(x) x$trio_mother == truth$dam & x$trio_father == truth$sire
data.frame(
  analysis = c("all pairs", "known crosses"),
  top_pair_correct = c(mean(right(a)), mean(right(ac))),
  significant_80 = c(mean(a$trio_significant), mean(ac$trio_significant)),
  correct_among_significant = c(mean(right(a)[a$trio_significant]),
                                mean(right(ac)[ac$trio_significant])))
```

Here random pairing produced about 60 of the 100 possible crosses, so the list
is not much shorter than all pairs and the gain is modest. It grows as the
design gets sparser: with each of ten dams crossed to three sires (30 of 100),
four four-allele loci, and six replicate populations, the top cross was right
for 82% of offspring against 58% when every pair was scored, and the share
assigned at 95% confidence rose from 20% to 63%.

## How to read the confidence

The Delta confidence is a population-level statement: it is calibrated on
average over the broodstock that *could* have been drawn from these allele
frequencies, not conditionally on the particular fish in this hatchery. Over 16
simulated hatcheries with five four-allele loci, precision among assignments at
80% and 95% was 85% and 95% (all pairs) and 83% and 96% (known crosses), as
stated. But the proportion of offspring whose top pair was right ranged from 64%
to 86% between hatcheries, because a particular set of parents can happen to be
genetically similar. With few parents and weak markers, check the realised
precision on known crosses where you can; the posteriors below were calibrated
in the same simulations (stated 0.969, observed 0.965 at a cutoff of 0.80).

## Posteriors and plausible sets

Because the crosses are a known, exhaustive list, each offspring also gets a
posterior probability over crosses. Every pair LOD is a ratio against the same
denominator, so differences between LODs are exact log-likelihood ratios
between crosses, and
$$\Pr(c \mid o) \propto \pi\, w_c\, e^{\mathrm{LOD}_c}, \qquad
  \Pr(\text{none} \mid o) \propto 1 - \pi,$$
with $\pi$ = `prop_sampled_crosses` and $w_c$ optional cross weights, for
example eggs fertilised. `trio_set` is the smallest set of crosses holding 95%
of the posterior: one cross when the data decide, several when they do not.

```{r}
head(ac[, c("offspring", "trio_mother", "trio_father", "trio_posterior",
            "trio_set_size", "trio_set")], 8)
table(set_size = ac$trio_set_size)
mean(mapply(function(s, m, f) paste(m, f, sep = " x ") %in% strsplit(s, "; ")[[1]],
            ac$trio_set, truth$dam, truth$sire))
```

When a set holds several crosses they are almost always half-sib crosses that
share one parent, and that is useful in itself: the shared parent is known even
when the cross is not.

## Family sizes

Summing posteriors over offspring estimates how many offspring each cross
produced, which feeds directly into estimates of family-size variance and the
effective number of breeders.

```{r}
fam <- attr(ac, "families")
fam$true <- as.vector(table(factor(paste(truth$dam, truth$sire),
                                   levels = paste(fam$mother, fam$father))))
head(fam[order(-fam$expected), ], 8)
cor(fam$expected, fam$true)
```

## Screens

Two screens drop weak or impossible comparisons before the best is chosen,
and both are applied inside the significance simulation too, so the critical
Delta describes assignments made under the same rule. `max_mismatch` removes
candidates excluded at more than that many loci; `min_loci` removes comparisons
resting on too few typed loci, so that a poorly typed offspring is left
unassigned rather than judged against a threshold simulated at average typing.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
as <- assign_trios(g, sim$offspring, freqs = p, error = 0.01,
                   crosses = crosses, nsim = 3000, nsim_trio = 1000,
                   max_mismatch = 2, min_loci = 4)
attr(as, "criteria")
```

## What is not modelled

The alternative to "this is the parent" is an unrelated individual. Close
relatives of the true parents among the crossed fish (common when broodstock are
themselves related) are not modelled in `assign_trios()`, and with weak markers
they can be mistaken for the parent; see `vignette("relatedness")`. The
posterior over crosses assumes that an offspring from no listed cross has two
parents outside the design, not one listed and one unlisted.

## References

Marshall, T.C., Slate, J., Kruuk, L.E.B. & Pemberton, J.M. (1998) Statistical
confidence for likelihood-based paternity inference in natural populations.
*Molecular Ecology* **7**, 639-655.
